title: Adopting Memory-Safety and Fine-Grained Compartmentalisation with CHERI
gist: David Chisnall of SCI Semiconductor argues CHERI is not an ISA but a family of localizations (Morello on Arm, CHERIoT for microcontrollers, RVY being standardized for RISC-V) that teach hardware what a pointer is, delivering spatial and temporal memory safety for C/C++ via recompilation rather than rewrites. His deeper thesis is that isolation is a solved problem and the real unsolved one is a programming model for sharing — CHERI's answer being pointer-passing that replaces RPC serialization with object-graph sharing, enabling thousands of compartments and a 350-instruction trusted switcher whose import/export tables make security policy statically auditable.

themes.theme: Isolation is solved; sharing is the hard problem

insights.claim: Isolation between fully separated workloads is a solved and cheap problem — MMUs and VMs have done it for decades and separate physical CPUs are the cheapest answer — so the genuinely hard architectural problem is workloads that must communicate, which is what dictates hardware design and programming model.
insights.speaker: David Chisnall
insights.so_what: A diagnostic for evaluating any new hardware security feature: ask for the sharing programming model, not the isolation guarantee — most vendors have only the latter.
insights.quote: The place where this starts to get really difficult is when you have two workloads that are not fully isolated, where they need to communicate.
insights.locator: I'm going to say a lot of words very quickly

insights.claim: CPU vendors pitching new isolation techniques consistently answer the sharing-model question with 'we can put pages in both trust domains,' which is not a programming model — a decade-long pattern of the industry shipping isolation without usable sharing.
insights.speaker: David Chisnall
insights.so_what: Explains why a decade of hardware enclave/isolation features has seen thin developer adoption — the missing piece is ergonomics, not enforcement.
insights.quote: They say, we can put pages in both trust domains. You say, that's actually not a programming model.
insights.locator: This is a message that I've been trying to drum into CPU vendors

insights.claim: Process-based isolation as used by web browsers does not scale because of MMU indirect lookups and page tables and forces RPC frameworks with serialization and copying, topping out at a few tens of compartments while browsers actually want thousands to tens of thousands of sandboxes for per-image and per-audio-sample decoding and privilege-separated JITs.
insights.speaker: David Chisnall
insights.so_what: Quantifies the two-to-three order-of-magnitude gap between what current isolation hardware supports and what security-critical software actually needs — the addressable gap CHERI targets.
insights.quote: What they actually want is thousands to tens of thousands of sandboxes, and just none of the existing techniques work there.
insights.locator: How Did We Get Here?

themes.theme: CHERI is a family, not an ISA

insights.claim: There is no CHERI ISA — CHERI is an abstract set of ideas localized per architecture the way SIMD is (NEON/SVE on Arm, SSE/AVX on Intel), with existing localizations including research MIPS prototypes, Arm's Morello for Aarch64, and CHERIoT for microcontrollers.
insights.speaker: David Chisnall
insights.so_what: Reframes CHERI as a cross-architecture feature category rather than a competing ISA — meaning incumbents (Arm, RISC-V) can absorb it rather than be displaced by it.
insights.quote: You'll hear a lot of people talk about the CHERI ISA. There is no such thing as the CHERI ISA.
insights.locator: CHERI: What It Is, and What It Isn't

insights.claim: A RISC-V CHERI base called RVY is in the final stages of standardization, adding an open-ISA localization alongside Arm's Morello.
insights.speaker: David Chisnall
insights.so_what: RISC-V standardization is the gating event for broad CHERI silicon availability — a concrete milestone to track for the memory-safety hardware thesis.
insights.locator: We're currently in the final stages

insights.claim: CHERI adoption strategy is deliberately bifurcated: application cores from mobile to data center scale need binary compatibility because people hold gigabytes of existing binaries, while microcontroller developers will happily recompile — which is why CHERIoT could assume CHERI throughout the whole hardware and software stack.
insights.speaker: David Chisnall
insights.so_what: Embedded/microcontroller is the near-term commercial beachhead for CHERI; application-core adoption is gated by the far harder binary-compatibility constraint.
insights.quote: If you say to embedded systems people, you need to recompile all your code, they say, ok, it's Tuesday.
insights.locator: For a lot of the CHERI work

insights.claim: CHERI unifies two previously disparate research lines — 1960s capability systems, where an unforgeable delegatable token of authority carries reducible permissions, and fat pointers, where a pointer carries metadata such as bounds and types.
insights.speaker: David Chisnall
insights.so_what: Positions CHERI as a synthesis of 60 years of prior art rather than novel research risk — relevant to assessing technical maturity.
insights.locator: CHERI started with unifying a set of ideas

insights.claim: CHERI's core move is teaching hardware that pointers are a real thing rather than a language-level abstraction: pointers cannot be created from thin air, they carry bounds and permissions, and every load, store and jump instruction now takes a hardware-protected capability instead of a bare address.
insights.speaker: David Chisnall
insights.so_what: The distinguishing mechanism versus software mitigations — enforcement moves below the compiler, so it applies to all code including hand-written assembly and third-party binaries.
insights.quote: CHERI teaches the hardware that pointers are actually a thing.
insights.locator: I'm actually going to start explaining what CHERI is

insights.claim: A CHERI capability doubles pointer size — 64 bits on a 32-bit system, 128 bits on a 64-bit system — with bounds compressed via a floating-point representation where displacements to top and bottom share an exponent, so larger objects require stronger alignment, a constraint memory allocators already satisfy.
insights.speaker: David Chisnall
insights.so_what: Pointer doubling is the primary hardware cost of CHERI, and the compression scheme is what keeps it at 2x rather than 3x — relevant to memory and cache budgeting.
insights.locator: CHERI Capabilities

insights.claim: The permit-load-mutable permission enables deep immutability: handing over a pointer to a tree's root node with that permission removed means every pointer loaded during a full traversal has store permission stripped, granting a read-only view of the entire reachable graph in one operation.
insights.speaker: David Chisnall
insights.so_what: Deep immutability over object graphs is exactly the primitive that RPC serialization exists to fake — its availability in hardware is what collapses IPC cost.
insights.locator: We can enforce a deep immutability property

insights.claim: A single non-addressable tag bit per capability-sized word in physical memory, mirrored in the register file, gives a one-bit dynamic type system where everything is either a pointer or not, and any partial overwrite implicitly clears the tag — which blocks the pointer-injection step common to most attack primitives.
insights.speaker: David Chisnall
insights.so_what: Names the specific attack step neutralized: attacker-controlled data read from network or file can never be dereferenced as a pointer.
insights.quote: A lot of first or second steps in attack primitives involve overwriting a pointer with something attacker controlled. If that's something you've read from the network or from a file, now it's not a pointer, so you can't dereference it.
insights.locator: If we then try and dereference that

insights.claim: Capability tags propagate through type-oblivious copies, which is the property that makes memcpy implementable — a requirement most academic C memory-safety retrofits fail because they assume a compiler pass can statically identify where all the pointers are.
insights.speaker: David Chisnall
insights.so_what: A concrete falsification test for competing memory-safety schemes: ask whether they handle memcpy without annotation.
insights.quote: you've not compiled any non-trivial C with your tool, have you?
insights.locator: This is really important because this property

insights.claim: CHERI capability properties are strictly monotonic — bounds can only be narrowed and permissions only removed — so recovering a wider pointer requires re-deriving it from another source rather than expanding an existing one.
insights.speaker: David Chisnall
insights.so_what: Monotonicity is the invariant that makes downstream guarantees (revocation, compartment isolation, auditing) sound; it is the property to check any CHERI-like scheme against.
insights.locator: Critically, all of these are monotonic

insights.claim: The sealing mechanism lets any compartment vend type-safe opaque handles as direct pointers, replacing file descriptors and kernel-managed indirection tables and enabling a fully privilege-separated least-privilege design where no central kernel owns the handle table.
insights.speaker: David Chisnall
insights.so_what: Removes the kernel from the handle-brokering path — the structural reason CHERI can scale to thousands of compartments where microkernels cannot.
insights.locator: I said I'd come back to the sealing mechanism

insights.claim: CHERI bounds and permission checks execute before MMU address translation and compose cleanly and orthogonally with it, so CHERI is additive to existing virtual memory rather than a replacement.
insights.speaker: David Chisnall
insights.so_what: Orthogonality to the MMU lowers the integration barrier for existing OS and silicon vendors — a key adoption-risk reducer.
insights.locator: What does this look like in your memory hierarchy?

insights.claim: On larger CHERI systems the capability program counter plus a default data capability let you build a programming model closely resembling WebAssembly — arbitrary code confined to a region of address space with no access outside it — while unmodified legacy binaries still run with metadata treated as implicit.
insights.speaker: David Chisnall
insights.so_what: A hardware-native WebAssembly-equivalent sandbox without a runtime — potentially undercutting the case for software sandboxing layers on CHERI-capable silicon.
insights.locator: On the larger systems, the combination of these two

themes.theme: Recompile, don't rewrite: the economic argument

insights.claim: Adopting CHERI requires essentially no C source change: the compiler emits a bounds-setting instruction after the stack allocation so a classic off-by-one store at index 14 of a 14-element array deterministically traps instead of overwriting the return address.
insights.speaker: David Chisnall
insights.so_what: Zero-source-change adoption is the entire commercial thesis — it makes memory safety a build-flag decision rather than a rewrite budget.
insights.quote: As a C programmer, the most important thing about adopting CHERI is you don't really have to do anything.
insights.locator: Adopting CHERI Doesn't Change C

insights.claim: A small university team ported a FreeBSD kernel, Wayland compositor, KDE and an app suite — roughly 100 million lines of C and C++ — to run fully memory safe under CHERI, whereas rewriting the equivalent in a memory-safe language would cost at least tens and maybe hundreds of billions of dollars, if not trillions.
insights.speaker: David Chisnall
insights.so_what: The core cost-comparison against the rewrite-in-Rust strategy; if directionally right, it reframes memory safety as a hardware capex decision rather than a decade of software labor.
insights.quote: If you imagine the equivalent effort to rewrite all of that code in a memory safe language, that's just at least tens and maybe hundreds of billions of dollars, if not trillions to get to that point.
insights.locator: This lack of change is how we can do things

insights.claim: The CHERI team abandoned an annotated C dialect where only selected pointers became capabilities because it demanded enormous source changes, and found that making every pointer a capability actually lowered programmer cognitive overhead — a tcpdump port went from a 1,700-line diff for partial protection to a four-line diff for full memory safety.
insights.speaker: David Chisnall
insights.so_what: A hard-won lesson with general applicability: partial/opt-in safety schemes carry higher migration cost than blanket ones — a heuristic for evaluating gradual-typing and gradual-safety products.
insights.quote: That was 1,700 lines of diff. We then rewrote that to be fully memory safe for everything, and that turned out to be a four-line diff.
insights.locator: We did a tcpdump port

insights.claim: Memory safety alone addresses roughly 70% of security vulnerabilities, and adding compartmentalization on top is what pushes coverage toward 80%, 90% and close to 100%.
insights.speaker: David Chisnall
insights.so_what: Sets the ceiling on memory-safety-only approaches (including language rewrites) at ~70% and identifies compartmentalization as the remaining 30% — a segmentation of the security tooling market.
insights.locator: From Memory Safety to Compartmentalization

insights.claim: The industry's excitement about the 70% memory-safety figure caused it to largely forget compartmentalization, which was the original goal of the CHERI project when it started 15 years ago.
insights.speaker: David Chisnall
insights.so_what: The under-hyped half of the technology is the one its creators consider the point — where differentiated value likely sits versus commodity memory safety.
insights.quote: Let's get very excited about that, and sort of forgot a little bit about compartmentalization. That was what we were doing it for to start with.
insights.locator: Then everyone said, memory safety bugs

themes.theme: Temporal safety by revocation instead of GC

insights.claim: Temporal memory safety is the genuinely hard problem because pointers to an object can be anywhere in memory with no way to enumerate them, and CHERI inverts garbage collection's contract: instead of the object surviving until the last pointer goes away, all pointers go away when the object does.
insights.speaker: David Chisnall
insights.so_what: Preserves the C malloc/free abstract machine while getting GC-grade safety — the design choice that avoids forcing a language change on existing codebases.
insights.quote: We're doing the logical dual of that and saying, when the object goes away, all pointers to that also go away.
insights.locator: CHERIoT Temporal Safety

insights.claim: CHERIoT implements deterministic use-after-free with a shadow bitmap of one bit per 8-byte allocation granule (16 bytes on larger systems), a hardware load filter that clears the tag when a loaded capability's base maps to a freed granule, and a background hardware state machine that sweeps memory so freed regions become reusable after a full revocation scan.
insights.speaker: David Chisnall
insights.so_what: Deterministic rather than probabilistic UAF elimination in hardware, with quantified metadata overhead (1 bit per 8 bytes) — the hard spec to compare against MTE-style probabilistic tagging.
insights.locator: The first building block we have for this

insights.claim: Revocation is safe to base on the capability's base address because monotonicity guarantees a derived pointer's base always stays within the original allocation's bounds, with the only corner case being zero-length capabilities that are harmless because they cannot be dereferenced.
insights.speaker: David Chisnall
insights.so_what: Shows how one architectural invariant (monotonicity) makes an otherwise expensive graph-walking problem into a constant-time lookup — the leverage point of the whole design.
insights.locator: It's safe to use the base address for that

themes.theme: A 350-instruction trusted base and auditable compartments

insights.claim: In a CHERI system a protection domain is simply the transitive closure of memory reachable from the capabilities in a register file, so two threads with different register files are already two protection domains within a single address space.
insights.speaker: David Chisnall
insights.so_what: Compartments become nearly free to create — the mechanism that makes thousands-of-sandboxes architectures feasible where per-process isolation cannot go.
insights.quote: the set of reachable memory is the transitive closure of the memory reachable from the capabilities in your register file
insights.locator: From Memory Safety to Compartmentalization

insights.claim: CheriBSD adds a coexecve system call that creates a new OS process without a new address space and installs a chosen set of root capabilities, allowing a tiny in-address-space executive to implement shared objects or pipe-like channels roughly one to two orders of magnitude faster than traditional pipes by avoiding page pinning, bounce buffering and MMU translation pivots.
insights.speaker: David Chisnall
insights.so_what: A 10-100x IPC speedup with an incremental deployment path is the kind of concrete win that drives OS-vendor adoption independent of the security argument.
insights.locator: there's a very simple incremental deployment path

insights.claim: The CHERIoT RTOS switcher — the equivalent of a microkernel, handling context switching and cross-compartment calls — is about 350 instructions, compared with the roughly 200 unverified instructions seL4 advertises within a ~10,000-line verified microkernel, and CHERI's memory safety and absence of arbitrary-memory escape hatches makes verifying those 350 substantially easier.
insights.speaker: David Chisnall
insights.so_what: A trusted computing base measured in hundreds of instructions is a step-change versus conventional kernels — the strongest technical claim for safety-critical and regulated embedded markets.
insights.quote: This is about 350 instructions.
insights.locator: The really critical bit is the switcher

insights.claim: The CHERIoT scheduler must be trusted only for availability, not confidentiality or integrity: the switcher hands it a sealed capability to the register save area, so the scheduler can starve a thread but cannot see any interrupted thread's stack or register file.
insights.speaker: David Chisnall
insights.so_what: Decomposing trust by property (availability vs. confidentiality) rather than by component is a reusable architecture pattern for shrinking what must be verified.
insights.quote: The scheduler has to be trusted for availability by design. It's the thing that chooses which thread runs next, so it can choose to never run your thread if it hates you.
insights.locator: We have a scheduler

insights.claim: A CHERIoT compartment is essentially two registers — program counter capability for code and read-only data, and global pointer for mutable globals — plus an import table that is the only region permitted to hold capabilities not derived from those two, which forces the linker to record every external reference a compartment holds.
insights.speaker: David Chisnall
insights.so_what: The import-table constraint is what converts runtime security posture into a statically enumerable artifact — the basis of the auditing tooling.
insights.locator: Maybe now's a good time to say what a compartment is

insights.claim: Cross-compartment calls zero all unused argument registers, truncate the stack to the unused region and zero it on both call and return, so all sharing is explicit and all non-sharing implicit — eliminating the lookaside MPU or MMU policy that engineers must otherwise reason about.
insights.speaker: David Chisnall
insights.so_what: Explicit-sharing-by-default removes an entire class of configuration-error vulnerabilities that plague MPU/MMU-based embedded security.
insights.quote: That's really important because all sharing is explicit. All non-sharing is implicit.
insights.locator: It's going to truncate the stack

insights.claim: Exposing a function as a compartment entry point requires only annotating the prototype with the exporting compartment's name, with the call site completely unmodified — the compiler turns it into a direct call or an import-table entry depending on whether the compilation unit's compartment matches.
insights.speaker: David Chisnall
insights.so_what: Compartmentalization at annotation-level cost, roughly analogous to Windows DLL import/export attributes, is what makes retrofitting compartments to existing code economically viable.
insights.locator: What does this look like in C?

insights.claim: Because every external reference passes through the import table, CHERIoT ships Rego-based policy tooling that can answer questions like which compartments may open network connections and to which endpoints, and whether unencrypted data can leave the device by asking who may call send in the TCP/IP stack — with pass/fail policies wired into CI or code-signing flows.
insights.speaker: David Chisnall
insights.so_what: Turns supply-chain security from source review into a machine-checkable policy gate — the practical answer to trusting third-party embedded libraries.
insights.quote: assume this library that I got from this totally trustworthy North Korean person on GitHub is maybe malicious. What's the worst that can happen?
insights.locator: Auditing - Who Can Make Network Connections, and Where?

insights.claim: Each compartment carries a hash of every section it contains, allowing compartment-level policy to be tied to SBOM infrastructure so a sensitive capability can be bound to an exact binary from an auditable reproducible-build chain.
insights.speaker: David Chisnall
insights.so_what: Links hardware compartment boundaries to software supply-chain attestation — the enforcement teeth that SBOM programs currently lack.
insights.locator: There's also the hash of every section

insights.claim: Going beyond recompile-level memory safety to fully defended compartmentalized interfaces — including the ability to restart a crashed compartment from scratch — typically costs an additional 1% to 3% of code.
insights.speaker: David Chisnall
insights.so_what: A hard cost estimate (1-3% additional code) for the compartmentalization tier — the number to underwrite when modeling CHERI migration budgets.
insights.locator: Summary

themes.theme: Performance: microbenchmark cost vs. system-level win

insights.claim: CHERI's runtime overhead is dominated not by bounds checks — which run fully in parallel on the load-store pipeline and add essentially nothing — but by doubled pointer size, which is under 1% of memory for pointer-light workloads and as much as 10% to 20% for desktop workloads, plus explicit bounds-setting instructions.
insights.speaker: David Chisnall
insights.so_what: The cost model is memory-footprint-driven, meaning cache and store-buffer sizing is the design lever silicon vendors must pull, not check logic.
insights.locator: Questions and Answers

insights.claim: macOS's XPC framework for RPC between mutually distrusting processes copies transmitted data seven times including the kernel copy in and out, whereas a CHERI system needs zero copies, or one if the receiver does not trust the sender.
insights.speaker: David Chisnall
insights.so_what: Concrete baseline showing how much of current IPC cost is a workaround for the absence of safe pointer sharing.
insights.quote: It copies the data that you're sending seven times, including the kernel copy in and out.
insights.locator: How many people here have written code on macOS?

insights.claim: An unoptimized CHERI implementation may cost a few percent in microbenchmarks while producing factor-of-1,000 speedups at the system level, and matching CHERIoT's security on non-CHERI hardware such as FreeRTOS with protected tasks and defensive copying at every boundary would carry roughly ten times the overhead — which is why nobody actually does it.
insights.speaker: David Chisnall
insights.so_what: Reframes the CHERI performance debate: the honest comparison is against equally secure non-CHERI systems, which nobody builds because the cost is prohibitive.
insights.quote: We're talking about things that on an unoptimized implementation may be a few percent performance cost in microbenchmarks, leading to a factor of 1,000 speedups on system-level things.
insights.locator: Questions and Answers

insights.claim: Apples-to-apples CHERI performance comparison is structurally impossible because no vendor will invest equal design effort in a CHERI-optimized and a non-CHERI-optimized processor to run side by side.
insights.speaker: David Chisnall
insights.so_what: Treat any published CHERI overhead number — favorable or unfavorable — as methodologically contested; the decision has to rest on the system-level argument.
insights.quote: It is the worst question to try and answer because you're never able to do an apples-to-apples comparison.
insights.locator: Questions and Answers
